title: The Subjunctive
description: The subjunctive mood: purpose with ἵνα, future conditions with ἐάν, and the hortatory subjunctive.

blocks.caption: Summary
blocks.html: The subjunctive has only a present and an aorist (in the New Testament). It always takes primary endings, joined by the long variable vowel ω/η instead of ο/ε. The aorist subjunctive has no augment: it is made on the unaugmented aorist stem (λύσω, λίπω, λυθῶ). The tenses of the subjunctive differ not in time but in kind of action: the present for continuing or repeated action, the aorist for the action as a simple event. Its negative is μή.

blocks.caption: Aorist subjunctive
rows: The second aorist subjunctive has the same endings on the second aorist stem: λίπω, λίπῃς, λίπῃ. The present subjunctive of εἰμί is ὦ, ᾖς, ᾖ, ὦμεν, ἦτε, ὦσι(ν).

blocks.caption: Uses
blocks.html: - Hortatory: the first person plural urges: πιστεύσωμεν, let us believe; μὴ ἁμαρτάνωμεν, let us not sin. - Purpose: ἵνα with the subjunctive, in order that: ἦλθεν ἵνα σώσῃ ἁμαρτωλούς. - Future condition: ἐάν with the subjunctive, if (in future time): ἐὰν ἴδῃ τὸν κύριον, πιστεύσει. A condition about the present or past takes εἰ with the indicative: εἰ ἐλάβομεν ταύτην τὴν ἐντολήν.

blocks.caption: Common confusion
blocks.html: λύσω is both the aorist subjunctive (that I may loose) and the future indicative (I shall loose); λύσῃ is aorist subjunctive active third singular or future middle second singular. The construction (ἵνα, ἐάν, or a main verb) decides.
